extracted.intended_audience: advanced_undergraduate/graduate students and researchers in combinatorics and graph theory
extracted.subtask_description: Techniques and constructive criteria for proving enumerative combinatorics results (trees, partitions, Latin squares) and for constructing/completing combinatorial objects. Covers bijections, linear-algebraic counting, recurrences, double counting, formal power series, and constructive completion algorithms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bijective proof (Prüfer / Joyal approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Find a bijection from the set of labeled trees on n vertices onto a set of known cardinality (e.g., sequences (a1,...,a_{n-2}) with 1 ≤ ai ≤ n, giving n^{n-2}, or Joyal's bijection to N^N giving n^n for trees with two distinguished ends).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit encodings are required. Prüfer code: encode each labeled tree uniquely as a sequence of length n−2 (classical). Joyal's construction: represent a map f:N→N as a directed graph G_f, identify the union M of vertices on directed cycles, order those cycle-vertices via their preimages to obtain left and right ends, draw the path through f(a),...,f(z) and attach remaining vertices according to their paths to the path; this correspondence is reversible. A successful bijection must be explicit and invertible (construct both directions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Linear-algebraic counting (Kirchhoff / matrix-tree theorem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Count spanning trees of a connected simple graph G using the determinant of a matrix derived from an oriented incidence matrix (M = C C^T); for any i, t(G) = det M_{ii} (matrix with i-th row and column deleted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct incidence matrix B with rows V and columns E, orient edges to replace one 1 by −1 producing C, set M = C C^T. Use the Binet–Cauchy theorem to expand det M_{ii} as sum over (n−1)×(n−1) minors; show minors equal ±1 exactly when the corresponding edges form a tree and 0 otherwise (use leaf-deletion triangularization). For K_n evaluate resulting matrix to obtain n^{n−2}. Proofs must justify the ±1/0 determinant claim and the Binet–Cauchy application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recurrence and induction (Riordan–Rényi style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Set up a recurrence for a more general counting function (here T_{n,k}: number of labeled forests on {1,...,n} with k trees and a specified k-set A having its vertices in distinct trees), derive a relation, and solve it by induction to obtain closed form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive combinatorial recurrence by considering degree of a distinguished vertex: T_{n,k} = sum_{i=0}^{n-k} C(n−k,i) T_{n−1,k−1+i} with base conditions T_{0,0}=1, T_{n,0}=0 (n>0). Use induction and algebraic manipulation (binomial sums, index changes) to arrive at T_{n,k} = k n^{n-k-1} and hence T_n = n^{n-2}. The recurrence must be combinatorially justified and boundary conditions specified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double counting via rooted forests (Pitman's method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Count the same set two different ways: consider rooted forests Fn,k (forests with k rooted components) and define refining sequences F1,...,Fk with Fi ∈ Fn,i and Fi contains Fi+1. Count sequences by starting from a tree and by starting from a fixed Fk to deduce counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show N*(Fk) (number of refining sequences ending in Fk) equals N(Fk)(k−1)! (deleting edges) and also equals n^{k−1}(k−1)! (constructing by adding edges, n choices for vertices and appropriate choices for roots). Equate to deduce N(Fk)=n^{k−1}. Use this to compute |Fn,k| and then T_{n,k}. The argument must carefully count orders (deletion sequences vs addition choices) and justify independence of choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal power series (generating-function) manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat infinite products and series as formal power series (ignore convergence) and manipulate products like ∏_{k≥1} 1/(1−x^k) to read off combinatorial counts (e.g., p(n) partitions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret factors: 1/(1−x^k) = 1 + x^k + x^{2k} + ... counts multiplicity of part k; coefficient of x^n equals number of partitions p(n). Use algebraic identities on products (e.g., cancellation of even factors, substitution y = −1) to derive combinatorial equalities (e.g., po(n) = pd(n), or parity identities). When using this method, explicitly state combinatorial interpretation of each factor and justify coefficient extraction operations formally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Glaisher's bijection (odd parts ↔ distinct parts)
rubrics_metrics.description: A constructive bijection between partitions into odd parts (Po(n)) and partitions into distinct parts (Pd(n)): write multiplicities of each odd part in binary and split accordingly to obtain distinct even-multiples of the odd parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given λ with multiplicities n_i for odd part λ_i, write n_i in binary and replace by sums 2^{a}λ_i to produce distinct parts. Verify distinctness (highest power of 2 factor distinguishes parts) and give inverse: group distinct parts by highest power of 2 to recover odd multiplicities. Provide explicit examples and check invertibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Involution/bijective proof for Euler pentagonal theorem (Bressoud–Zeilberger involution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide an involution φ mapping partitions in P(n − b(j)) to partitions in P(n − b(j±1)) so that coefficients c(k) in ∏(1−x^k) are supported only at generalized pentagonal numbers with alternating signs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define φ on λ:λ1+...+λt by two cases depending on inequality t+3j ≥ λ1; apply prescribed transformation (shift/add/drop ones) to move partitions between P(n−b(j)) and P(n−b(j±1)). Verify φ is an involution or pairs off partitions so unmatched sizes correspond to pentagonal indices. The bijection must be explicit and checked to produce the desired cancellations leading to the pentagonal theorem expansion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of auxiliary variable to track statistics (y-variable trick)
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce an extra variable y in generating functions (∏(1+ y x^k)) to keep track of auxiliary statistics (e.g., number of distinct parts), then specialize (e.g., y = −1) to obtain parity/combinatorial identities (Ed(n) − Od(n) etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret coefficient of x^n y^m as number of partitions of n into m distinct parts. Setting y = −1 gives alternating counts Ed(n) − Od(n) and comparing to known product expansions yields combinatorial parity results. Make explicit the combinatorial meaning of y and justify specialization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation of analytic identities into partition combinatorics (Rogers–Ramanujan type)
rubrics_metrics.description: Translate infinite-product/q-series identities into partition-theoretic statements (e.g., partitions with parts ≡ 1,4 (mod 5) correspond to partitions with part-difference ≥ 2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret the product side as restriction on allowed part residues and the sum side as restrictions on differences/gaps. Provide combinatorial statement (f(n)=g(n)) and, if available, bijective proof; if not, note that analytic proofs may exist while bijections can be difficult or highly nontrivial (Garsia–Milne).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and necessary condition for partial Latin square
rubrics_metrics.description: A partial Latin square of order n is an n×n array with some cells filled from {1,...,n} such that every symbol appears at most once in every row and column; this is a necessary condition for extendability to a full Latin square.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before attempting completion, verify the prefilled cells already satisfy the Latin constraints (no repeated symbols in any row or column). Counterexamples (small numbers of filled cells that block completion) show that satisfying the local condition is necessary but not always sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjugacy principle for Latin squares
rubrics_metrics.description: Viewing a Latin square as a (3×n^2) line-array (rows, columns, elements), one may permute the three lines (and permute symbols inside lines) to obtain conjugate Latin squares. A partial Latin square can be completed iff any conjugate can be completed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use conjugacy to transform a given partial configuration into a more convenient form for completion (e.g., move filled cells into top rows). Completion of the conjugate and undoing the conjugation yields a completion of the original. This justifies reductions in proofs by rearrangement of roles (rows/columns/elements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 1 (extend r×n Latin rectangle via Hall's theorem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any (r×n)-Latin rectangle with r < n can be extended to an ((r+1)×n)-Latin rectangle (hence completed) by finding a system of distinct representatives for sets of missing symbols per column.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let A_j be the set of symbols not used in column j; each |A_j| = n−r and every symbol is present in precisely n−r of the A_j, so m chosen columns contain m(n−r) symbol-occurrences and thus at least m distinct symbols, satisfying Hall's condition. Use SDR to construct the (r+1)-st row. When applying, explicitly form the sets and verify Hall's criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 2 (completion when ≤ n−1 prefilled cells with constrained distribution)
rubrics_metrics.description: A partial Latin square of order n with at most n−1 filled cells (and an additional distribution constraint allowing a reduction) can be completed to a Latin square.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use conjugacy to assume filled entries occupy the top r rows with row-fill counts f1≥...≥fr and Σ f_i ≤ n−1. Fill rows sequentially using Hall's theorem on carefully chosen sets A_j (symbols missing in target row and not present in considered columns), and establish inequalities bounding unions of A_j (inequality (1) and then (2) in the text) to verify Hall's condition for all m. The proof requires checking combinatorial inequalities derived from the f_i; follow the step-by-step union-size estimates from the source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smetaniuk constructive completion algorithm (Evans conjecture proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: A constructive inductive method that completes any partial Latin square with at most n−1 filled cells by row/column permutations, reduction to order n−1, and a sequence of swaps inserting the missing symbol n appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steps: (1) By conjugacy and permutations move filled cells so all filled cells lie below the diagonal except a single occurrence of symbol n placed on the diagonal. (2) Remove symbol n and ignore first row and last column to get an order n−1 partial square with ≤ n−2 filled cells; apply induction to complete it. (3) For k = 2,...,n−1, put value n in cell (k,n) then swap n with diagonal entry x_k at (k,k). If x_k was not present in last column, done for that k; if it was present, further adjustments are made as prescribed in the constructive process. Verify at each step no future column will be altered for already-fixed k. The algorithm is explicit and constructive; to use it, follow the permutation and swap schedule and check conflicts as described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple forced/constructive completions (examples and heuristics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Special easy cases: if first n−1 rows are filled and last is empty, completion is forced by placing each missing symbol in its missing column; if only first row is filled, complete by cyclically rotating entries in subsequent rows (cyclic Latin square).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these base-case constructions as illustrations or base steps in induction or as sanity checks. They exemplify when completion is unique (forced) vs when many completions exist (degrees of freedom).
